title: A set, and an array as a hash table
sub: Longest Consecutive Sequence and First Missing Positive: O(n) without sorting and without extra memory
cards/0/title: Longest Consecutive Sequence: the problem and its signals
cards/0/body:
Longest Consecutive Sequence (LeetCode #128). Given an unsorted integer array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers — values x, x + 1, x + 2, …, wherever they sit in the array. [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] → 4 (the run 1, 2, 3, 4). n ≤ 10⁵, values up to 10⁹ in absolute value, and the statement demands O(n).

Signals: neighbours in a run are partners by exact value (for x they are x − 1 and x + 1), and the question “is that number present?” means a set. And “O(n)” in the statement explicitly rules out sorting.

Without that constraint the honest answer is sorting plus one pass that skips duplicates: O(n log n). It is worth naming as the baseline.

A set, head-on: put everything into a HashSet and from every number count upwards while the next one is in the set.
cards/1/q: How many Contains checks does the head-on set approach make on the array [1, 2, 3, …, n]?
cards/1/options/0: ≈ n²/2 — from every number we walk to the end of the run
cards/1/options/1: ≈ n — every number is checked once
cards/1/explain: From 1 the loop walks the whole run, from 2 one number less, … from n just one. The sum n(n + 1)/2 ≈ n²/2: for n = 10⁵ that is 5·10⁹ checks. The work repeats: every number of a run walks its tail again.
cards/1/wrong/1: Each number would be checked once if we counted only from the start of a run. Here counting starts from every number.
cards/1/wrong/2: There is nowhere for a logarithm to come from: no halving, no sorting. Every start walks the run linearly.
cards/2/title: Count only from the start of a run
cards/2/body:
The repeated work is the tail of a run: every number of the run walks it again. But a run only needs counting once — from its first number. And the first number is recognized in O(1): x starts a run if x − 1 is not in the set.

Why O(n). The inner while starts only from run starts and walks each run once; runs do not overlap, so all the while loops together make at most n steps. Plus one x − 1 check per number. O(n) time in total: a nested loop does not by itself mean O(n²) — count how many times the body runs in total. Memory is O(n) for the set.

Iterate over the set, not the original array: each number is in the set once, so each run start is counted once as well.
cards/3/explain: Iterate over set: each number once. A run start is a number without x − 1; the rest are skipped with continue. Then grow len while x + len is in the set. With x + 1 in the while the loop would never end: the condition does not change from step to step.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on [5, 2, 99, 3, 1, 4, 100]. The set is walked in the same order: 5, 2, 99, 3, 1, 4, 100. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does with the next number.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Skip it: 4 is in the set
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The first number of the set is 5. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: 5 − 1 = 4 is in the set, so 5 is not a run start: continue. The run that contains 5 will be counted by its first number — we will get there.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Skip it: 2 is in the set
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: x = 1. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: 0 is not in the set — 1 starts a run. The while walks 2, 3, 4, 5 and stops at 6: length 5. Skipping 5 earlier removed nothing from the set — continue only declined to count from it. The record was 2 (99…100), now it is 5. We check x − 1, not x + 1: almost every number has a successor.
cards/5/q: This code gives the right answer, but on an array of 1, 2, …, 50 000 plus another 50 000 ones it exceeds the time limit. Tap the line responsible.
cards/5/explain: The loop walks nums, which holds 50 001 ones — and each of them starts a run, since there is no 0 in the set. Every one walks the run 1…50 000 again: about 2.5·10⁹ checks. The set holds a single 1, and the run is counted once. The fix is foreach (int x in set).
cards/6/title: First Missing Positive: an array instead of a set
cards/6/body:
First Missing Positive (LeetCode #41, hard). Given an unsorted integer array, find the smallest positive number that is not in it, in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. [3, 4, −1, 1] → 2, [1, 2, 0] → 3, [7, 8, 9] → 1.

Observation: n numbers can occupy at most n of the values 1, 2, …, n. So the answer lies in 1..n + 1, and numbers ≤ 0 or > n can be ignored. With a HashSet it is easy: put everything in and check 1, 2, … — O(n), but O(n) memory too. Sorting is O(n log n).

Idea: a set over the keys 1..n is a bool[n] array, and we already have an array of length n — the input itself. Let value v live in slot v − 1. For every i, while a[i] is a number from 1..n that is not in its place, swap it with the contents of slot a[i] − 1. A new number arrives at position i, and it needs placing too — hence while, not if. Then the first slot i without “its own” number i + 1 gives the answer; if everything is in place, the answer is n + 1.

Why O(n): every swap puts one number into its place for good, and there are n places — so there are at most n swaps in total. The condition a[a[i] − 1] != a[i] (“the target slot does not hold this number yet”) protects against duplicates: on [1, 1] with the check a[i] != i + 1 the two ones would swap forever.

In a game: the smallest free save slot number or id is the same problem.
cards/7/task: Step through the trace on [3, 4, −1, 1, 6, 2]. The slots are labelled #1…#6: slot #v must hold v (index v − 1 in the code). The rig stops twice and asks what happens next.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Move on to the next i: this i already had a swap
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: The pointer is on slot #2: 4 has just left for slot #4, and 1 arrived here. What next?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: The while checks this slot again: 1 is within 1..6, and slot #1 holds −1, not a one. Swap: 1 takes its place, −1 arrives in slot #2 and stays — it is outside 1..n. With an if the 1 would stay in someone else’s slot, and the answer would come out wrong. The answer is searched for only after the placement, in a second pass.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: The placement is done: [1, 2, 3, 4, −1, 6]. What does the method return?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: The second pass looks for the first slot without its own number: #1…#4 are in place, #5 holds −1. The answer is 5. n + 1 = 7 would be the answer only if all of 1..6 were in their places.
cards/8/q: On [3, 4, −1, 1] this code returns 1, while the right answer is 2. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/8/explain: The if makes one swap and moves on, while the number that arrived at position i stays unplaced. At i = 1: 4 leaves for slot #4, 1 arrives — and stays in slot #2, while #1 holds −1. The second pass sees −1 in #1 and answers 1. A while places the arriving number too.
cards/9/body:
Missing Number (#268): numbers 0..n, one is missing. Placement would work, but arithmetic is simpler: n(n + 1)/2 minus the array’s sum (keep the sum in a long) — or XOR, covered in the bits unit.

Find All Duplicates (#442): values 1..n, each appears once or twice. Marking by sign: for each v make slot |v| − 1 negative; if it is already negative, v has been seen. The sign is a spare bit in the slot, no second array needed.

The array must not be modified. Placement and marks spoil the input. Ask the interviewer; in production code a method that silently reorders someone else’s array is a bug. Then be honest: a HashSet or a copy of the array, O(n) memory.

Keys are dense and bounded — tile ids 0..10⁴, slot numbers, enemy indices in a pool: a bool[] instead of a HashSet<int>. No hashes, no buckets, one byte per key (or one bit in a BitArray).
cards/10/q: You solve First Missing Positive out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: can the array be modified, what values occur, how much memory is allowed
cards/10/items/1: Observation: the answer lies in 1..n + 1, other numbers do not matter
cards/10/items/2: Name the simple solutions: HashSet — O(n) memory, sorting — O(n log n)
cards/10/items/3: Idea: the array is its own set — value v goes into slot v − 1
cards/10/items/4: Write the code: a while with a swap, the condition via the target slot a[a[i] − 1] != a[i]
cards/10/items/5: Run [3, 4, −1, 1] and state the complexity: at most n swaps, O(n) time and O(1) memory
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: duplicates, all of 1..n in place (answer n + 1), negative and huge values
cards/10/explain: First agree on whether the input may be spoiled — that decides whether placement is allowed at all. The 1..n + 1 observation is the key to the whole problem: without it, it is not obvious that an array of length n is enough. Explain the complexity through the number of swaps, not through nested loops.
cards/11/title: The cost of a set, and when an array is enough
cards/11/body:
A HashSet<int> of 10⁵ numbers is a bucket array plus an entry array (hash, next, value): about 16 bytes per element plus headroom up to a prime size, around 1.6 MB. Every Contains is a jump to a random place in memory, and for large n the cache misses show more than O(1) promises. Hence an honest conclusion: O(n) with a set is not always faster than O(n log n) with sorting — sorting an int array walks memory sequentially. In an interview name both options and their cost; in a project, measure.

When keys are dense and the range is known, no set is needed at all: an array of flags by index is the same “hash table” where the hash is the number itself.
cards/11/deep:
HashSet internals. In modern .NET HashSet<T> is built like a Dictionary without values: the same buckets and entries, prime sizes. The constructor from a collection, new HashSet<int>(nums), takes its capacity from the collection’s Count right away, and if duplicates left the arrays 3 or more times larger than the number of entries, it calls TrimExcess() itself. HashSet has EnsureCapacity since .NET Core 2.1 and .NET Standard 2.1 (in Unity since 2021.2).

Sparse set. When you need O(1) add, remove and contains as well as a fast walk over the occupied keys only (active entities, selected units), use a pair of arrays: dense holds the keys contiguously, sparse[key] is the key’s position in dense. Contains: sparse[k] < count && dense[sparse[k]] == k; remove: move the last element of dense into the removed one’s place and fix its sparse. No hashes, no allocations, iteration over a dense array. Component storage in a number of ECS libraries is built on this structure.

Unity: Jobs and Burst. The com.unity.collections package has NativeHashSet<T> and NativeBitArray — a set and a bit array outside the managed heap, usable from Burst; release them with Dispose(). For dense keys the bit array beats the hash set there too.

Proof for First Missing Positive. Let P be the number of slots holding “their own” value. A swap in the while puts a[i] into slot a[i] − 1, which did not hold its own value yet, and touches no slot that already does (slot i does not hold its own, otherwise the condition is false). So every swap increases P by 1, and P ≤ n — there are at most n swaps over the whole algorithm, and at most 2n checks of the while condition.

The sign-marking variant of #41: first replace every number ≤ 0 or > n with n + 1, then for every v in 1..n make slot v − 1 negative; the first positive slot i gives the answer i + 1. Also O(n) and O(1), with no swaps — easier to prove.

If the input must stay untouched and memory counts: take the copy from ArrayPool<int>.Shared.Rent(n) (available in .NET Standard 2.1 and in Unity). The array may be longer than n — work with the first n elements — and give it back with Return in a finally. In hot code, after warm-up, that is zero new allocations.
cards/12/q: Match the condition with the technique.
cards/12/pairs/0/0: Length of a run of consecutive numbers in O(n)
cards/12/pairs/0/1: HashSet, count only from x without x − 1
cards/12/pairs/1/1: Value v goes into slot v − 1
cards/12/pairs/4/0: Keys are dense ids from 0 to 10⁴
